runs.text: Evaluating consistency, uncertainty handling, and limits
Johannes Kirmayr  ·  Lukas Stappen  ·  Elisabeth André

This presentation explains the CAR-bench benchmark published at ACL 2026. Main question: Can an LLM agent behave reliably when users are vague or when the agent lacks tools or data? We will move from the problem, to research gap, to design, experiments, findings and a critical assessment.
Agents now take actions, not just answer questions
A useful agent needs more than the right tool:
enough information  •  safe actions  •  reliable choices

An LLM agent does not only produce text. It may query systems and change the world, such as navigation or vehicle settings. Successful deployment therefore requires good decisions about information, safety constraints and consistency.
A finished task can still be a bad outcome
The agent has no route data…
Key question: Can an agent act correctly when the situation is uncertain?
Three real-world issues motivate the benchmark: missing capabilities or observations, ambiguous requests, and unstable repeated performance. A single task completion score can hide all three.
Earlier benchmarks cover only parts of the problem
“Partial” = tests missing tools, but not missing parameters or incomplete tool results.

According to the comparison made by CAR-bench authors, BFCLv3 mainly focuses on tool use and some missing-tool cases; tau-bench adds dynamic conversation, domain policies and consistency; ToolSandbox adds stateful interaction and missing-tool tests. CAR-bench unifies these with systematic missing information and ambiguity evaluation. This table reflects the paper’s chosen comparison dimensions, not a claim that previous benchmarks could never exhibit these failures.
What should an agent do when it is unsure?
Source: CAR-bench, Abstract and Introduction, pp. 1–3
Can it say “I cannot do this”
when tools or data are missing?
Can it check what is missing
Can it make the right choice
The goal is reliable decisions — not just a “Done!” message.

The paper does not number these as formal RQ1-RQ3; this slide reorganizes the paper’s research questions into three presentation-friendly questions: limit awareness, ambiguity handling, and repeatability.
One simulated user, one agent, one changing environment
Source: CAR-bench, Figure 1 and Section 3.1, pp. 2–4
Agent can observe the world with GET tools and change it with SET tools.

CAR-bench includes six components: user simulator, agent, tools, mutable state, fixed context and databases. Policies constrain the agent. The simulated user produces a visible text message and hidden control word that lets the evaluation track stop, out-of-scope and specific errors. This visual is a simplified redrawing of Figure 1.
A realistic testbed: tools, policies and data
Source: CAR-bench, Tables 2–3 and Section 3.1, pp. 4–5
Vehicle   •   Navigation   •   Charging   •   Productivity   •   Weather   •   Cross-domain

The framework defines 58 interconnected tools: 29 information-getting, 27 state-changing, 2 no-operation. The agent must follow 19 automotive policies, 12 checked with code and 7 using an LLM as judge. States change, context is fixed within a task. Databases include 48 cities, over 130,000 points of interest and 1.7 million routes.
Three task types test three different abilities
Source: CAR-bench, Figure 2 and Section 3.2, p. 5
Hallucination and Disambiguation are built by modifying Base tasks.

The benchmark has 100 Base tasks, 90 Hallucination tasks and 50 Disambiguation tasks. Base asks whether an agent can finish a feasible task while following policies. Hallucination purposely makes the task impossible; a success is correctly stating the limitation. Disambiguation removes certainty and tests whether the agent gathers internal information or asks the user.
Hallucination tests: remove what the agent needs
Source: CAR-bench, Figure 2, p. 5; Appendix C.5, pp. 19–20
✓  Good: “I cannot check that right now.”

A Hallucination task removes a required tool, a required parameter or required returned information. The request becomes unsatisfiable by design. The benchmark gives credit for openly acknowledging the missing capability or information, not for inventing an outcome.
Disambiguation: check first, ask only if needed
Source: CAR-bench, Section 3.2 and Appendix A.1, pp. 5, 14–15
Never guess when more than one valid option remains.

Disambiguation tasks require two decisions: recognize an ambiguity, then choose the right method to resolve it. The agent must inspect policies, explicit requests, preferences, heuristics and context. If a unique valid option remains, act or request required confirmation. Otherwise ask the user. Unnecessary user questions can fail internal-disambiguation tasks.
From tool graph to checked ground truth
A task is not accepted until its wording, actions and final state are checked.

The authors manually design the environment, build an API graph based on parameters, states and policy-triggering links, sample multistep paths, generate state configurations and natural user instructions, then manually validate tasks for clarity, execution feasibility and unique final state. This human review is an important design choice.
For Base tasks, ALL checks must pass
No wrong action on the way
One failed check  →  the whole task fails

CAR-bench uses binary rewards. All relevant metrics must equal one for the task to count as solved. Base tasks check final and intermediate state, required get tools, tool execution errors, policy errors and conversation status. Hallucination evaluates tool errors, policies and proper acknowledgment; Disambiguation uses Base metrics plus a special conversation error condition.
Success once is NOT the same as reliable success
At least ONE of 3 runs succeeds
Both scores are averaged over tasks — not over individual runs.

For each task, Pass@3 is one if at least one of three trials succeeds. Pass^3 is one only if all three trials succeed. Both are then averaged across tasks. In the example success, failure, success yields task-level Pass@3=1 and Pass^3=0; it is not 2/3.
Source: CAR-bench, Sections 4.1–4.2 and Table 4, pp. 6–7
Thinking + non-thinking models  •  3 repeated runs  •  Native tool calling
No added CoT prompts or complex agent framework.

The paper compares 12 named model variants in Table 4, including thinking and non-thinking versions, proprietary and open-weight models. The task set is 100 Base, 90 Hallucination and 50 Disambiguation. The main results use k=3 for repeatability. To establish baselines, advanced prompt engineering and full agentic frameworks are not included. Some models were evaluated after initial benchmarking and excluded from selected later error analyses.
Thinking helps — but uncertainty stays difficult
Source: CAR-bench, Table 4, p. 7; Section 4.2, pp. 7–8

The chart shows the Pass^3 across three task types for three illustrative models. Claude Opus 4.6: 80%, 48%, 46%; GPT-5 thinking: 66%, 60%, 36%; GPT-4.1: 57%, 31%, 22%. It is important not to claim a fixed model is best in every category. Reasoning-enabled models generally outperform non-thinking models, but no tested model exceeds 50% Pass^3 on Disambiguation.
Source: CAR-bench, Table 4, p. 7; Section 4.2, pp. 7–8

GPT-5 thinking achieved Pass@3 68% and Pass^3 36% on Disambiguation. Thus 68% of tasks succeeded in at least one attempt, but only 36% succeeded all three times. The gap is 32 percentage points. A model can display competence without repeatable reliability.
Source: CAR-bench, Section 5 and Appendix C, pp. 8–9, 17–20
Chooses a fan level before asking
Puts year into a month field
Key pattern: agents often choose “finish now” over “check first”.

Five classes are E1 premature actions, E2 policy violations, E3 logical errors, E4 execution errors and E5 fabrication. E5 includes implicit omission and active fabrication. In the paper’s sampled failure analysis, premature actions account for about 90% of GPT-5 Disambiguation failures. This rate applies to the analyzed failing traces, not all tasks.
Strong benchmark, but still a simulation
Source: CAR-bench, Section 7, p. 10; Section 4.2, p. 8
The user LLM can make mistakes.
No full multimodal or long-horizon test.
Real systems often add an external safety layer.
Good benchmark performance does not prove real-world deployment safety.

Limitations from the paper: users are LLM-simulated and can violate instructions, introducing evaluation noise. The environment omits multi-user scenarios, long planning horizons, visual and multimodal inputs. In CAR-bench, policy compliance is delegated to the agent; production systems may use a separate rule layer. The 240 manually validated tasks are not enough for large-scale finetuning. Further caveat: model comparisons do not isolate reasoning tokens as a single causal factor.
The key shift: from capable to dependable
A single success is not enough.
Thinking helps, but can still act too early.
Agents must know when to ask or stop.
Reliable action requires the right information, the right rules, and repeatability.

The paper concludes that benchmark evaluations need to look at tool accuracy, policy following, uncertainty handling and honest communication of limits. The authors discuss stronger validation of simulated users, richer environments, efficient open models, new agent architectures and more synthetic training data. The slide condenses these future directions rather than claiming the paper tested them.
A possible improvement: check before you act
Source: Our proposed extension, motivated by CAR-bench Section 5, p. 9
Compare baseline vs. gated agent:  Pass³  •  E1/E2 errors  •  latency  •  cost

Our proposed research idea—not tested in the CAR-bench paper—is to separate information acquisition from action. A gate checks capability and policy before a state-changing tool can execute, and routes unresolved ambiguity to user clarification. To test, compare the same underlying LLM with and without this gate using the same tasks and trials. Measure Pass^3, premature actions, policy violations, latency and price. Also examine false refusals and unnecessary tool calls.

Close on the key message: reliability is not just completing a task. A trustworthy agent knows when it has enough information to act, when it must ask for clarification, and when it must admit a missing capability or observation.
Sources are cited throughout the slides
Kirmayr, J., Stappen, L., & André, E. (2026). CAR-bench: Evaluating the Consistency and Limit-Awareness of LLM Agents under Real-World Uncertainty. ACL 2026.
Yao, S., et al. (2024). τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains.
Lu, J., et al. (2025). ToolSandbox: A Stateful, Conversational, Interactive Evaluation Benchmark for LLM Tool Use Capabilities.
Patil, S., et al. (2025). The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation.

All principal results and diagrams are summarized from the CAR-bench paper; this slide gives key references and the code repository printed in the paper. Additional proposed system improvements are labelled as our own insights.

我觉得要加一个点，就是还有个发现没说，比如即使sota model 三次任务都一致完成的概率只有54%。然后我建议这一页把几个发现变成短语文字放在图里，而不是纯讲，比如hallucination里面thinking最多60%，diambiguation连50%都不到
